t: Deniz Tek: ‘Top Gun may have got the name of Val Kilmer’s Iceman from me’
lede: The Radio Birdman guitarist on his time in the US Marines, selling a guitar to Keith Richards and getting texted by Anthony Albanese

img.cap: ‘My squadron mates always say I’m the original Iceman’ … Deniz Tek of Radio Birdman on stage in 2016. Photograph: Jordi Vidal/Redferns

p.b: Have you ever had a nickname, and what is it?

p: When I was in the US Marines F-4 Phantom squadron, Iceman was my call sign, which is given to you on your first operational deployment. You have it on your helmet and a patch on your flight suit. One day, a film crew came to visit our squadron, doing research for a film they were working on, and they hung out with us for two weeks.

A year and a half later, the movie comes out, and it’s Top Gun. The story got started that they got the name of Val Kilmer’s Iceman character from me. Most likely it was already written into the screenplay, but who knows? My squadron mates always say I’m the original Iceman.

p.b: Apart from buying and playing Fred “Sonic”Smith’s guitar for your whole career, you once sold a guitar to Keith Richards. Tell us about that.

p: I lucked into getting into their inner circle when they were in Sydney in 1973. I was 20. I had a guitar, a 1958 National Baron. I knew Keith liked those guitars, so I rang up his guitar tech and asked him if he thought Keith might be interested in having it. He said, “Oh God yeah, bring it around after the show.” That guitar was my ticket to the top three floors of the Hyatt Kingsgate in Kings Cross. I hung out all night and had the most mind-blowing time. I wanted to trade the guitar for one of his, but that didn’t work out; he just gave me some money for it.

p.b: What album do you always return to, and why?

p: The first one that comes to mind is James Brown, Live at the Apollo in 1963. From the moment the needle hits the groove, it’s pure excitement – the Godfather of Soul in his early days, hitting his peak. Usually live albums are disappointing, I think, but that one’s not. It just jumps out and hits you like you’re right there.

p.b: Is it true that during your ER days in Newcastle, Australia, you delivered a baby by the name of Daniel Johns, later of Silverchair?

p: There’s a grain of truth to it, but it wasn’t Daniel, it was Chris [Joannou, Silverchair’s bassist]! I didn’t find that out until they invited me to record a cover of

with them in New York, and they asked me when I was doing obstetrics at the Mater. And that’s how I found out I was around when Chris was born. I don’t remember him as a baby specifically, but it’s definitely possible that I attended his birth.

p.b: You live in Hawaii and grow coffee on your own farm. What’s your coffee order?

p: When I’m overseas, it’s a cortado, and when in Australia, a piccolo.

p.b: What’s the oldest thing you own, and why do you still have it?

p: I have some fossils that are 60m or 70m years old, and I just keep them around because it’s cool to have something that you can hold in your hand that’s that old.

As far as something that I actually acquired, I guess it would be the T-shirt that Keith Richards gave me on that tour. And in those days, they didn’t have merch – there was no such thing as merch! – but their crew had tour T-shirts identifying what they did, and I asked for one of those.

Keith said, “Wait a minute,” and he goes over to his bag, and it was like this little carry-on. It was tiny, and he’s pulling out these amazing pieces of clothing. It was blowing my mind to even see this stuff. And he pulled out this T-shirt, and he says, “Here, you can have this.” It was a T-shirt from their 1966 tour of the United States.

p.b: What’s the weirdest thing you’ve ever eaten?

p: Ants on toast at a high-end restaurant in Melbourne. And I loved it!

p.b: Who’s the most famous person in your phone?

p: Anthony Albanese. Before he was PM, he would sometimes come to our gigs. He’d text me if it was last minute and we were sold out. We always welcomed him backstage. He would chat with me, have a beer off the rider. He was a great supporter of the band, even in parliament.

After he became PM he still came to see us a couple of times, once at the Factory theatre in Marrickville and once at the Manning Bar. The security detail had to be accommodated, obviously. That coordination was done via our manager and the venues.

p.b: Have you ever called him direct?

p: No, I would never do that!

p.b: What song do you want played at your funeral?

p: The Carnival is Over by the Seekers. And Ray Charles’ Let the Good Times Roll.

p.b: What’s the best lesson you’ve learned from someone you’ve worked with?

p: In music, it was from [producer] Charles Fisher, who taught me to go with my instinct and trust that above all else. In medicine, it was a guy called Greg Henry. He said in medicine, people think it’s all about healing and curing, and it’s not. He said, “Our job is to manage often, cure occasionally, but care always.”
Also, Scotty Asheton [the Stooges drummer] once told me: “Never tell the truth in an interview.”

p.i: • Full Throttle by Deniz Tek is out now (Picador; $36.99)
